source: Inoue et al. (2025) Wider or Deeper? Scaling LLM Inference-Time Compute with Adaptive Branching Tree Search (AB-MCTS, NeurIPS 2025 spotlight)
finding: Equal generation budget of 27 calls, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3. Standard LATS-style MCTS was not clearly better than plain repeated sampling, and was worse on ARC-AGI. Adaptive-branching MCTS (Thompson sampling, not UCT) had the best average rank.
numbers: Pass@1 LiveCodeBench GPT-4o / DeepSeek-V3: repeated sampling 37.8 / 40.7; standard MCTS 36.7 / 43.2; AB-MCTS-M 38.9 / 43.0. CodeContest: RS 37.9 / 43.2; MCTS 37.5 / 43.8; AB-MCTS-M 40.6 / 44.6. ARC-AGI Pass@2: RS 15.0 / 18.6; MCTS 9.0 / 14.0; AB-MCTS-M 12.3 / 16.0. Avg rank: RS 3.5, MCTS 4.2, AB-MCTS-M 2.3. Stds 0.3-3.6 points, 5 runs.
quote: repeated sampling proves to be a strong baseline in our setup, indicating the importance of broad exploration for this task
limits: Models are GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 (non-reasoning). Gains of 1-3 points are about one std. Baseline MCTS is LATS-style fixed width 3 at 27 nodes. Score signal is test-case pass rate, an executable checker.
agent_relevance: At small budgets, plain sampling is a hard baseline. A scaffold that tree-searches must beat equal-call repeated sampling, and wide exploration may matter more than depth.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) AB-MCTS, Appendix D (ARC-AGI-2, frontier reasoning models) and C.8/A.6 ablations
finding: On 120 ARC-AGI-2 public tasks with reasoning models (o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro, R1-0528), adaptive-branching search beat repeated sampling at the same number of LLM calls, more so beyond about 50 calls. Mixing models helped further. The search signal was the score on demonstration cases, an executable non-learned check.
numbers: Pass@k (coverage): o4-mini repeated sampling 23%; single-model AB-MCTS-A 27.5%; multi-LLM AB-MCTS over 30% (up to about 250 calls). Standard MCTS fixed width on LiveCodeBench DeepSeek-V3 Pass@1: w=3 0.429, w=5 0.432, w=10 0.402 (std 0.015-0.021). Prior hyperparameters of AB-MCTS: Pass@1 36.8-39.5, all within noise.
quote: the single-model AB-MCTS using o4-mini improved the success rate to 27.5%
limits: Pass@k, not Pass@2, so no selection step was scored. Single-run curves. 120 tasks, so 4.5 points is about 5 tasks. Appendix result.
agent_relevance: Closest evidence for gap 1: with a frontier reasoning model and a code checker, adaptive tree search gains about 4.5 points over equal-call sampling. The gain is modest and needs the checker.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) AB-MCTS, Section 3.2 (why UCT is dropped)
finding: The authors state UCT cannot be applied to LLM answer trees because the number of children is unbounded (a GEN node can always produce one more child) and unexpanded children have no score. They replace UCT with Thompson sampling over a Bayesian score model. Fixed-width MCTS is sensitive to its width hyperparameter.
numbers: Fixed width w=5 best on LiveCodeBench with DeepSeek-V3 (0.432 vs 0.429 at w=3 and 0.402 at w=10).
quote: The UCT score is inapplicable to our AB-MCTS because GEN nodes make the problem fundamentally different
limits: One benchmark, one model for the width sweep. No sweep of the UCT constant c itself.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the real tuning knob in LLM trees is width (children per node), not c. Prefer an adaptive wider/deeper rule or progressive widening over a fixed branching factor.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: PRM-guided search (best-of-N, beam, lookahead) on MATH with PaLM 2-S*. Beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets and falls to or below best-of-N at large budgets. On easy questions (bins 1-2) beam search over-optimises the verifier at higher budgets; on medium bins (3-4) it keeps helping. Lookahead (the MCTS-like method, no stochastic exploration) generally underperforms at equal generation cost. Compute-optimal allocation by difficulty matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute.
numbers: Difficulty = 5 quantile bins from pass rate over 2048 samples per question; budgets 4, 16, 64, 256 generations; lookahead cost counted as N x (k+1) samples. On easy and intermediate questions, test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model in a FLOPs-matched comparison; on the hardest questions there is little benefit.
quote: lookahead search is largely representative of how MCTS-style methods would be applied at test-time
limits: Oracle difficulty uses ground-truth correctness. Model-predicted difficulty (verifier average over 2048 samples) costs extra compute that the paper did not charge. MATH only, PaLM 2 with a trained PRM.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: difficulty predicts when search helps, but estimating difficulty is itself expensive. The paper calls this an open exploration-exploitation problem.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: Compares best-of-N, beam search and DVTS (diverse-subtree beam search) on MATH-500 and AIME24 over many policy sizes and PRMs. MCTS and lookahead were not run because of cost. Best method depends on policy size, PRM and difficulty. Quantile bins are poor because models differ, so they use absolute pass-rate thresholds (easy 50-100%, medium 10-50%, hard 0-10%).
numbers: Policies under 7B: best-of-N best on easy, beam search best on hard. 7B-32B: DVTS best on easy and medium, beam on hard. 72B: best-of-N best at every difficulty level. A 1B model with compute-optimal TTS exceeds a 405B model on MATH-500 (paper headline).
quote: for policy models with 72B parameters, BoN is the best method for all difficulty levels
limits: Math only, trained PRMs, no MCTS arm. Headline model comparisons depend on the PRM.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 6: as the base model gets stronger, the case for structured search over plain best-of-N weakens. A difficulty gate should depend on model strength, not a fixed question label.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1, Section G (unsuccessful attempts) and Section E.4
finding: Re-read this session. DeepSeek tried MCTS with a pre-trained value model for test-time scaling and for training. MCTS improved inference when paired with a pre-trained value model, but self-improvement through search did not scale. In the limitations text they call R1 more token-efficient than majority voting or MCTS because it allocates tokens by problem difficulty.
numbers: R1 AIME 2024 Pass@1 79.8%, Pass@64 90.0%, majority vote 86.7%. No MCTS accuracy number is reported.
quote: while MCTS can improve performance during inference when paired with a pre-trained value model, iteratively boosting model performance through self-search remains a significant challenge
limits: Qualitative negative result with no numbers, no ablation, no compute data. Not a controlled test of external MCTS on R1.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the only first-party statement. It says external MCTS can still help inference with a good value model, but internal long-CoT is the cheaper way to spend adaptive compute.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Long-CoT reasoning models (QwQ-32B-Preview, R1) spend large compute on easy problems with almost no accuracy gain. The first solution round is correct in the vast majority of cases. A self-training fix cuts tokens with no accuracy loss.
numbers: 2+3 question: o1-like models use 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. First solution correct in more than 92% of cases. MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview: 48.6% fewer tokens at equal accuracy (about 93%). 2 to 4 solution rounds for 76-80% of QwQ cases.
quote: contribute minimally to improving accuracy, lack diversity in reasoning strategies, and occur more frequently with simple problems
limits: Studies internal search of reasoning models, not external MCTS. Models are QwQ and R1. Test sets ASDIV, GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 5: supports a skip-search gate on easy items. Extra rounds of exploration on easy items are waste even inside the model.

source: Coquelin and Munos (2007) Bandit Algorithms for Tree Search (UAI)
finding: Proves UCT can be far too optimistic. On a deceptive tree where the best branch sits behind branches that look better early, UCT needs about D-1 nested exponentials of rounds before it first sees the best reward. With a square-root confidence bonus the transitory regret is still of order exp(exp(D)). Asymptotic regret is still O(log n) (or O(sqrt n)). They propose a modified UCT (bonus grows with depth) and BAST (smoothness).
numbers: Example tree: suboptimal branch gives reward (D-1)/D at every leaf; optimal branch gives 1. Time to first optimal reward is Omega(exp(exp(D))) for the square-root bonus and D-1 nested exponentials for the log bonus. Modified UCT regret is exponential in depth (order 2^D) but safe in the worst case.
quote: It takes Omega(exp(exp(D))) rounds to get the 1 reward!
limits: Theory with a constructed worst case, no LLM data. Whether natural reasoning trees look like this is untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, theory part now opened: a depth-greedy tree with a misleading early value can burn the whole budget. A scaffold should cap depth and keep some flat or restart sampling.

source: Feng et al. (2024) AlphaZero-Like Tree-Search can Guide Large Language Model Decoding and Training (TS-LLM, ICML)
finding: Learned value and outcome reward model. The PUCT-style constant c_init was chosen from only two values {0.3, 3.0} by a few trials, with no sweep reported. Wider trees help a lot. Tree search beats CoT-SC at equal tokens on Game24, ProntoQA, RLHF and chess endgame, but CoT-SC beats tree search on GSM8K at equal tokens, and tree aggregation gains less than CoT-SC on small problems.
numbers: Path@1 Game24 CoT 12.7, BFS-V 64.8, MCTS-alpha 63.3, MCTS-Rollout 71.3. GSM8K CoT-greedy 41.4, BFS-V 52.5, MCTS-alpha 51.9, CoT-SC-ORM 52.3. Game24 width text: performance almost doubles (43.8 to 80.7) with larger tree width (6 to 50). n_simulation 5 for shallow and 10 for deep trees; c_base 19652.
quote: we chose it by running several trials from two possible values
limits: Needs a trained value and ORM. The width table is partly garbled in the PDF text, so which method gives 80.7 is uncertain. Single seed.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the one source with any c choice tried only two values. Treat c as task-tuned; width and simulations per step carry more effect than c.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS), ablations Tables 8, 9, 11
finding: The only exploration-weight ablation found in an LLM-MCTS paper. On HotPotQA (n=5 children, k=50 trajectories), lowering w from 1 to 0.5 hurt; raising to 2.0 gave no gain but faster convergence. The authors say the optimum depends on the environment.
numbers: HotPotQA EM: w=0.5 0.55; w=2.0 0.63; default w=1.0, d=7 0.63 (Table 11; row-to-value order in the extracted text is partly ambiguous). Depth d=4 about 0.62. Table 9: ReAct best-of-250 0.42, CoT-SC k=250 0.40, ToT (n=5,k=50) 0.49, RAP 0.54, LATS n=1 0.48, LATS n=5 0.63. Tokens upon success: ToT 210,215, RAP 176,500, LATS 173,290.
quote: Increasing w to 2.0 does not lead to a performance improvement, but we tend to observe faster convergence.
limits: One task, one seed, 100 questions, no CI. Tokens reported only on successful runs, so failed-run cost is hidden.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 7: c between 1 and 2 is flat on HotPotQA; below 1 is worse. Report cost on all runs, not just successes.

source: Qi et al. (2024) rStar and Guan et al. (2025) rStar-Math: UCT constant and rollout budgets
finding: Both papers use plain UCT with a constant c that is not reported in the main text and no sensitivity sweep. rStar uses 32 rollouts; rStar-Math uses 16 rollouts per problem per round, then 64 for unsolved ones. rStar-Math accuracy saturates around 64 trajectories on MATH, AIME and OlympiadBench but still rises on College Math.
numbers: rStar: 32 rollouts, depth 8 on MATH. rStar-Math Table 6 MATH by round: base 58.8, R1 75.2, R2 86.6, R3 87.0, R4 89.4; AIME 0, 10.0, 43.3, 46.7, 50.0 (30 problems). With only 4 trajectories rStar-Math exceeds Qwen best-of-N baselines that use a 72B ORM.
quote: rStar-Math shows saturation or slow improvement at 64 trajectories
limits: Constant c not swept in either paper. rStar-Math rounds also change the policy and PPM, so the round curve confounds search with training.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no published sensitivity sweep of c in LLM MCTS beyond LATS w in {0.5, 1, 2}. Budgets of 16-64 rollouts are the practical range.

source: Guan et al. (2025) rStar-Math, reward-model ablation (Table 8) and round 1
finding: With the final round-4 policy, search driven by a process model beats best-of-N driven by an outcome reward model. A Q-value-regression PRM (PQM) is weaker on hard sets than the preference model (PPM). Round 1 used only terminal-guided annotation (final-answer match plus code execution, no learned reward) and already lifted MATH from 58.8 to 75.2.
numbers: Table 8, MATH / AIME / AMC / OlympiadBench: ORM best-of-N 82.6 / 26.7 / 65.0 / 55.1; PQM MCTS 88.2 / 46.7 / 85.0 / 62.9; PPM MCTS 89.4 / 50.0 / 87.5 / 65.3. Round 1 MATH 75.2, AIME 10.0, AMC 57.5. Round 2 (first learned PPM) MATH 86.6.
quote: both PQM and PPM outperform ORM by providing denser step-level reward signals
limits: Method (best-of-N vs MCTS) and reward type (ORM vs process) change together, so the table cannot separate them. Evaluation sets are small (AIME 30, AMC 40 problems). Training heavy.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the no-learned-reward round captured 16.4 of the 30.6 point MATH gain (58.8 to 75.2 of 89.4), but that is after fine-tuning. A scaffold-only agent cannot reproduce the fine-tuning part.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) ReST-MCTS*: LLM Self-Training via Process Reward Guided Tree Search (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Self-training on MCTS-found traces gives small and uneven gains. Averaged over MATH, GPQA-Diamond and CEval-Hard, the second ReST-MCTS* iteration on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct equals the few-shot baseline. Gains are clearer on Mistral and SciGLM. At 256 outputs, SC plus the ReST-MCTS value beat SC alone on GSM8K by 3.6 points.
numbers: LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct average: few-shot 28.99; ReSTEM iter2 26.83; Self-Rewarding iter2 27.73; ReST-MCTS* iter2 29.02. Mistral-7B average: few-shot 22.26; ReST-MCTS* iter2 26.50. SciGLM-6B average: base 33.63, iter2 35.90. Verifiers Mistral GSM8K / MATH500: SC 83.9 / 35.1; SC+ORM 86.6 / 38.0; SC+MATH-SHEPHERD 86.3 / 38.3; SC+ReST-MCTS 87.5 / 39.0.
quote: ReST-MCTS significantly outperforms other baselines despite insufficient budget
limits: Differences of 1-2 points on small sets (GPQA-Diamond has 198 questions). No seeds or CIs. Value and policy trained jointly.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the gain from training on MCTS traces is about 0 to 4 average points, so a no-training memory of traces should not be expected to match something that is itself marginal. No source tested trace memory directly.

source: Antoniades et al. (2025) SWE-Search: MCTS and iterative refinement for software agents (ICLR 2025), hyperparameter and cost appendix
finding: MCTS over repository tasks gave a 23% relative gain across five models, at several times the API cost. Default UCT c 1.41, about 5 expansions per node, about 100 iterations (Table 2 text is garbled, order inferred). The compute-matched Pass@5 table exists but its columns are scrambled in the PDF text.
numbers: API cost in USD, Moatless baseline vs SWE-Search (alignment inferred from a garbled table): GPT-4o 40.86 vs 576.00; GPT-4o-mini 9.90 vs 52.34; Qwen-2.5-72B 8.50 vs 42.50; DeepSeekCoderV2.5 3.66 vs 18.37; Llama-3.1-70B 9.00 vs 45.00. That is about 5x for four models and 14x for GPT-4o.
quote: Search-based exploration of multiple solutions results in higher computational costs.
limits: Row-column alignment of the cost and compute-matched tables is inferred; treat as approximate. SWE-bench Lite only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: on agent tasks the overhead is about 5x with a value agent and discriminator; the 23% relative gain must be weighed against it.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: With an automatic verifier, plain repeated sampling raises coverage log-linearly. Without one, majority vote and reward models plateau. This is the strong no-tree rival for gap 1.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples), above single-sample SOTA 43%. MATH Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%. 128 random problems each for GSM8K and MATH.
limits: Open 2024 models, no search or refinement arm.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: when a code or test verifier exists, the equal-token bar for MCTS is very high. Where no verifier exists, selection is the bottleneck, not generation.

source: Qi et al. (2024) rStar: mutual-consistency discriminator, plus rStar-Math terminal-guided annotation (non-learned value, synthesis of d11 and d12)
finding: Reward-free guidance works in a weak form. rStar picks the final answer by agreement between the generator's trace and a second small model that completes a masked partial trace. rStar-Math round 1 used answer match plus code execution. Neither paper isolates how much is lost versus a trained PRM at inference time.
numbers: rStar GSM8K: LLaMA2-7B 12.51 (few-shot CoT) to 63.91; Mistral-7B 17.89 (corrected CoT baseline) to 81.88; LLaMA3-8B-Instruct 74.53 to 91.13. rStar-Math round 1 (no learned reward) MATH 75.2 vs round 4 (PPM) 89.4.
limits: Read for the UCT section and results only. The fair rStar rival is SC@maj128 (23.05 / 52.84 / 67.55 / 84.69 / 88.68). No ablation swaps the discriminator for a PRM.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays partly open: independent-check guidance works in rStar, but the PRM-versus-checker gap at inference is not measured in anything found.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling, parallel vs sequential and REBASE
finding: On a 32B reasoning-tuned model, forcing the model to keep thinking (appending Wait) raised AIME24 from 50.0 to 56.7 and beat parallel majority voting on the non-reasoning base model. Rejection sampling for short traces showed inverse scaling. Tree search with REBASE and a 34B PRM scaled better than majority voting and even sequential scaling in their AIME24 test, but the reward-model compute was not counted.
numbers: AIME24 (30 problems): s1-32B no budget forcing 50.0, 2x Wait 53.3, best 56.7; MATH500 93.0; GPQA 59.6. Majority voting on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (64 samples) did not reach s1. 16 parallel trajectories for REBASE and majority voting. Budget forcing flattens after 6 forced continuations; 12 of 30 questions overran context at 512 steps.
quote: augmenting our model with REBASE scales better than majority voting, and even sequential scaling in this scenario
limits: The majority-voting baseline is the base model, not s1. AIME24 has 30 problems. REBASE token count excludes the reward model.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: for a reasoning model, internal sequential thinking is the cheap first lever. External tree search (REBASE here, not MCTS) still added on top, with uncounted verifier cost.

source: Synthesis for gap 6: balanced expansion beyond MATH (Wu et al. 2408.00724 as cited by the critique; Liu d05, Inoue d01, Feng d09)
finding: No source found that tests REBASE or step-level beam search against MCTS at equal tokens on planning, coding or agent tasks. Outside MATH and GSM8K the compute-matched evidence is: AB-MCTS on code and ARC (adaptive tree search roughly equal to or slightly above sampling), TS-LLM on Game24 and chess (tree search far above CoT-SC at equal tokens on deep problems), and Liu on MATH (best-of-N wins for a 72B policy).
numbers: See d01, d05, d09. Game24 equal-token with ORM: MCTS 69.34 at 649 tokens vs CoT-SC-ORM 50.6 at 684 tokens. GSM8K: CoT-SC-ORM 52.3 at 500 tokens vs BFS-V 52.5 at 485.
limits: 2408.00724 itself was not opened this session; the numbers come from the other papers. This line is a synthesis, not a source.
agent_relevance: Tree search seems to pay when the search is deep and an exact value exists (Game24, chess) and not on shallow arithmetic.
